question: The Ecodesign Directive (2009/125/EC)1 in combination with Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2024)2 sets energy efficiency requirements for refrigeration appliances with a direct sales function. A common practice for supermarkets is to order the body of a refrigerating cabinet separately from the doors and to assemble the cabinet in the store itself.

Fitted with the doors, the refrigerating cabinet complies with the Ecodesign requirements and in most cases is more energy efficient than single modules that often operate without doors. According to a recent interpretation by the Commission, the incomplete body of the refrigerator has to comply with the Ecodesign requirements.
This ignores, the fact that the refrigerator bodies are only ever used with doors and therefore, pushes innovative component manufacturers out of the market. 1.

Why does the Commission effectively prohibit the individual supply and combination of refrigerator bodies and appliance doors by customers even though the assembled refrigeration cabinet fully complies with the Ecodesign requirements and in most cases is superior in terms of energy efficiency?

Should legally relevant moment of ‘putting into service’ referred to in Article 381 of the Ecodesign Directive not be when the refrigerator is fully assembled as only at that point can compliance with ecodesign requirements be meaningfully assessed?
OJ L 285, 31.10.2009, p. 10–35, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/dir/2009/125/oj. OJ L 315, 5.12.2019, p. 313–334, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2019/2024/oj.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (23.3.2026) According to the relevant definitions, incomplete cabinets cannot be placed on the market or put into service as ‘refrigerating appliance with a direct sales function’ in the sense of Articles 2 of Commission Regulations (EU) 2019/20241 and (EU) 2019/20182, since some essential elements, for example doors, are missing.

Only products complying with the applicable requirements, either at the time of ‘placing on the market’ or ‘putting into service’, are subject to the Regulations. However, the fact that incomplete cabinets are not within the scope of the Regulations does not prevent free trade and supply on the market.

According to the Commission’s interpretation of the relevant rules, ‘putting into service’ should be understood as the moment at which economic operators need to demonstrate compliance with the applicable requirements. It is relevant, for example, for products which can only be used after an assembly, an installation or other manipulation has been carried out.

In case a body of a refrigerator is separately ordered from the doors, the natural or legal person who ‘puts the product into service’, has the same responsibilities as a manufacturer who ‘places a product on the market’. The Commission provides further information in the Blue Guide3.
It means that this natural or legal person must ensure that the product complies with the above-mentioned Regulations and that the appropriate conformity assessment procedure has been carried out.
